title: Ancillary variables
text:
Fluxes rarely explain themselves. CH₄ production, oxidation, and transport, and N₂O production and consumption, depend on water, oxygen (or redox state), temperature, substrate, vegetation, and, very often, human management. Ancillary measurements are also the predictors you will need for gap-filling and for comparing sites.

This page is a getting-started priority list distilled from committee discussions, including a working inventory of variables. It is not a mandatory protocol and not a substitute for ICOS or FLUXNET BADM metadata requirements. If you submit to a network, follow that network’s variable list (for ICOS, see the CH₄/N₂O instruction and the ICOS instructions for meteorological measurements, doi:10.18160/NHEG-4KWW). If you are just starting, measure the high-priority, feasible items for your ecosystem first.

The working inventory uses four priority levels:

Important and usually feasible
Important, but sometimes difficult
Useful wishlist, usually feasible
Useful wishlist, difficult

Items below are priority 1 unless marked otherwise.

title: Ancillary variables
text:
CH₄: a strong starting set

Meteorology and footprint

Incoming shortwave radiation
Air temperature
Wind speed and wind direction (needed for the flux itself and to interpret the footprint)
Air pressure (influences gas release from soils)
Precipitation (related to wetness and water-table dynamics)



Soil and water

Soil temperature at several depths, and in the main landscape types inside the footprint
Soil moisture, ideally as a profile and in more than one patch type (TDR or similar)
Redox state, or another redox index (priority 2: important, often harder)
Water-table elevation above or below the ground surface (priority 2; manual wells or a calibrated pressure transducer)
Water or profile temperature
Dissolved oxygen in soil or porewater, where it can be measured



Vegetation and carbon inputs

Ecosystem type
Vegetation density, especially plants with aerenchyma (priority 2). Aerenchymatous plants can vent CH₄ past oxidizing layers; some mosses and floating plants can instead favor oxidation.
Plant growth forms (rooting depth, height, LAI)
Cover of plants, open soil, and open water, including patchiness and the length of plant–water edges (aerial imagery or classification helps)
Gross primary production and the CO₂ flux, which help describe carbon supply to methanogens



More static site descriptors
Often priority 3, but still worth collecting:

Soil texture
Soil carbon and nitrogen content

title: Ancillary variables
section: CH₄: extras that depend on the ecosystem
text:
CH₄: extras that depend on the ecosystem
Marshes and tidal systems

Salinity (often essential where sulfate reduction competes with methanogenesis)
Tides and water-height variation; lateral carbon transport can be a large term

Peatlands

Drainage and rewetting
How much of the surface is ponded or affected by drainage (moisture topography)

Agricultural footprints

Manure type and amount, and how it is stored
Animal density and location in the footprint (enteric CH₄ as well as manure)
Animal diet, where it is known

title: Ancillary variables
text:
N₂O: a strong starting set
N₂O work is especially common in agriculture, but low-nutrient and peatland sites matter too.

Environment

Incoming shortwave radiation
Air temperature, soil temperature, and soil moisture
Precipitation (often the trigger for emission pulses)
Albedo and snow cover or snow depth, when freeze–thaw emissions are possible



Soil nitrogen and physical properties

Soil nitrate (for example, KCl extracts) and ammonium
Soil type and organic-matter content, C:N ratio, bulk density, and texture



Management
Write these down even if you cannot measure them with sensors at high frequency.

Fertilizer type and formulation, including inhibitors (product names can hide formula changes)
Total nitrogen applied, and total ammoniacal nitrogen if the source is manure
Fertilization date, and the gap between fertilization and the next wetting event
Planting date, crop or plant type (including legumes), tillage, and application method
Irrigation timing
Harvest yields and plant nitrogen content, which help close an agronomic nitrogen budget



Other settings

In low-nutrient (oligotrophic) systems, regional ammonia concentrations or nitrogen deposition can matter even without fertilizer
Peatland drainage and land-use history
Dissolved oxygen in soil

title: Ancillary variables
text:
How to use this list

Start with what you can sustain. A water-table record and a soil temperature and moisture profile will help almost any CH₄ site; fertilizer timing and soil moisture will help almost any agricultural N₂O site.
Match spatial sampling to the flux footprint. One point sensor in a heterogeneous marsh can mislead you.
Keep management as metadata, even when it is not a continuous sensor stream.
Look at metadata templates early. If your goals include carbon accounting or comparison with other FLUXNET sites, review the network’s BADM / metadata templates early so you do not have to reconstruct a season after the fact.

title: Ancillary variables
text:
What comes next
The ancillary-variables group has discussed a future white paper aimed at people entering CH₄ and N₂O eddy covariance. It would focus on terrestrial systems (agriculture, forests, tropics, peatlands, and other wet soils) and on the possible use of satellite products alongside tower data. Accompanying CO₂ fluxes are also useful for modeling. Until that paper exists, treat this page as a concise starting list rather than a final standard.
Back to: Guide overview

title: High-frequency data collection and processing
text:
High-frequency processing is everything that turns raw sonic-anemometer and gas-analyzer records into a 30-minute flux. The building blocks you may know from CO₂ still apply: coordinate rotation, time-lag correction, detrending or high-pass filtering, air-density (WPL) terms where needed, spectral corrections, and quality flags. CH₄ and N₂O change the emphasis because the signal is often weaker and more intermittent.

For the full system-setup specification (sensors, inlet geometry, calibration, maintenance), see the ICOS CH₄/N₂O instruction and Nemitz et al. (2018). Raw-data processing for CO₂ and energy fluxes is covered in Sabbatini et al. (2018), doi:10.1515/intag-2017-0043. This page covers the issues that most often surprise people new to non-CO₂ fluxes.

title: High-frequency data collection and processing

The building blocks you may know from CO₂ still apply: coordinate rotation, time-lag correction, detrending or high-pass filtering, air-density (WPL) terms where needed, spectral corrections, and quality flags. title: High-frequency data collection and processing
text:
Instruments and setup
These are complementary notes, not a sensor list.

Closed-path laser spectrometers are widely used for both CH₄ and N₂O. Pay attention to tube length, flow rate, and how you will find the time lag relative to the sonic anemometer.
Open-path CH₄ analyzers (including the LI-COR LI-7700) involve a well-known trade-off: open-path systems need larger air-density corrections, while closed-path systems can lose high-frequency signal in the tube under some conditions. See Detto et al. (2011), Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, doi:10.1016/j.agrformet.2011.05.014.
Network rules come first. As a matter of ICOS network policy, ICOS no longer accepts the LI-7700 at ICOS Class 1 ecosystem stations. If you are part of ICOS, follow ICOS. If you are not, treat instrument choice as a scientific and practical decision, follow your own network’s rules, and document your reasoning. This site does not ban any commercial sensor.
Record what you will need later: gas mole fractions, the three wind components, sonic temperature, and the diagnostics your analyzer provides (signal strength, flow, cell or mirror status, and so on).

title: High-frequency data collection and processing
text:
Time lag
For closed-path systems, detecting the time delay between the sonic anemometer and the analyzer is one of the most important high-frequency steps, especially when fluxes are small. When the signal-to-noise ratio is low, a lag search over a wide window tends to lock onto noise and can bias fluxes. Langford et al. (2015), Atmospheric Measurement Techniques, doi:10.5194/amt-8-4197-2015, is a good introduction to time-lag determination and detection limits for low signal-to-noise eddy-covariance data.
Points emphasized in committee discussions:

Detect time lags carefully for closed-path laser spectrometers.
Use a predetermined, relatively narrow lag-search window together with a default (nominal) lag, rather than letting the search wander over a wide window at every interval.
High-pass filtered lag correction, as implemented in eddy4R, is one documented approach.

title: High-frequency data collection and processing
text:
Wavelets and data retention
Conventional stationarity and turbulence flags can remove a large fraction of CH₄ or N₂O records at sites where fluxes arrive in short events. Wavelet-based methods are being used in this community to retain more high-quality data and to identify disruptive events, without treating every non-stationary period as unusable. Think of wavelets as a promising and actively used approach, not a required standard.

title: High-frequency data collection and processing
section: Despiking, spectral corrections, and quality flags
text:
Despiking, spectral corrections, and quality flags

Despiking. Remove physically impossible spikes in the raw data before averaging, but be careful not to treat real emission pulses (ebullition, fertilizer bursts) as noise.
Spectral corrections. These can become large when tubes, filters, or analyzers attenuate high frequencies. Intervals with extreme correction factors are often filtered later, at the half-hourly stage.
Quality flags. Standard flux quality flags, such as the Mauder and Foken (2004) scheme based on steady-state and integral-turbulence-characteristics (SSITC) tests, are still commonly applied. Many groups keep quality classes 0 and 1 for quantitative work.

title: High-frequency data collection and processing
section: Software people use at this stage
text:
Software people use at this stage
EddyPro (LI-COR; the processing engine is open source) is the processing software most widely used in this community to compute 30-minute fluxes from raw files. Other groups use in-house MATLAB, R, or Python code, or research pipelines such as eddy4R.
Whatever you choose, write down your settings: the lag window and nominal lag, the despiking method, the spectral corrections, and whether a default CO₂-style outlier filter was left on.

title: High-frequency data collection and processing
text:
A short high-frequency checklist

Confirm clock synchronization between the sonic anemometer and the gas analyzer (see ICOS for recommended practice).
For closed-path systems, document the inlet position relative to the sonic anemometer, the tube length, and the flow rate.
Set a physically plausible lag-search window and a nominal lag.
Inspect lag detections on days with clear fluxes and on days with near-zero fluxes.
Review raw-data diagnostics (signal strength, flow, analyzer warnings) before you trust a long automated run.
Record software versions and processing settings so the 30-minute product is reproducible.

Next: Half-hourly processing →

title: Work
text: The committee has been working since 2024 to turn scattered CH₄ and N₂O processing practice into shared guidance, open tools, and, over time, updates to community datasets such as FLUXNET-CH₄.

title: Work
text:
Three work areas
The work is organized into three structured areas, each with its own page in the guide:

High-frequency preprocessing of raw eddy-covariance data, including time-lag handling and methods that can retain more high-quality records.
Half-hourly post-processing: quality control of 30-minute fluxes, the still-open question of u* filtering for CH₄ and N₂O, gap-filling, and uncertainty.
Ancillary variables, launched after a full-committee discussion in September 2024, to identify which extra measurements most help people interpret and gap-fill non-CO₂ fluxes.

A longer-term goal is alignment with ONEFlux, the community processing pipeline used for FLUXNET carbon and energy products. For FLUXNET-CH₄ version 2.0, the group has committed to machine-learning approaches to gap-filling.

title: Work
text:
Timeline


April 2024 Committee work is underway, and the four objectives are in place.


September 2024 A full-committee discussion launches the ancillary-variables work area.


21–23 October 2024 FLUXNET-CH₄ v2.0 Data Processing Workshop in Berkeley, held as a hybrid meeting with more than 100 participants.


2024–2025 Groups share high-frequency processing approaches, including wavelet methods and time-lag correction, and work on machine-learning gap-filling pipelines.


July 2025 Updates presented at the FLUXNET Workshop in Brisbane.


November 2025 Status update in the FLUXNET Community Council newsletter.


2026 A Volkswagen Foundation workshop in Hannover on advancing data processing, including scoping toward a community position paper.


April 2026 Status: continue finalizing best-practice guidance, synthesize ancillary-variable recommendations, support new sites, and connect this work to the broader FLUXNET Data System Initiative (whose public data-system release was noted as December 2025).

title: Work
text:
Workshops

FLUXNET-CH₄ v2.0 Data Processing Workshop, Berkeley, 21–23 October 2024 (hybrid; more than 100 participants).
FLUXNET Workshop, Brisbane, 2025.
Volkswagen Foundation workshop on advancing data processing, Hannover, 2026.

Forthcoming: paper from the 2026 Volkswagen Foundation workshop (Hannover). Citation and link will be added when available.

title: Work
text:
Scientific progress
Progress so far is real but still developing. In brief:

High-frequency preprocessing. Wavelet approaches can retain records that conventional stationarity or turbulence flags would otherwise discard. There has also been work on time-lag detection for closed-path laser analyzers, including high-pass filtered lag correction as implemented in tools such as eddy4R.
Machine-learning gap-filling. Pipelines are being integrated for community use. Results were still preliminary at the time of the 2026 summary, so no performance numbers are reported here.
Low and negative fluxes. An active discussion addresses how to handle small and negative fluxes, which matter for upland sites and for the upland–wetland continuum, not only for large wetland sources.

title: Work
text:
Open challenges
The committee has been candid about what is hard:

Coordinating a global volunteer group across many time zones.
Balancing new methods against the need for a standardized, comparable product.
Developing robust uncertainty quantification for CH₄ and N₂O, which is not as settled as it is for CO₂.

title: Work
text:
Where the work is heading
The near-term path described in 2026 is to consolidate guidance (including this public getting-started site), develop synthesis and position papers, and keep moving FLUXNET-CH₄ version 2 toward a community-wide release that new sites can join.

title: Getting started with FCH₄ and FN₂O
text:
This site is a public, getting-started package for researchers who want to add eddy-covariance methane (FCH₄) and nitrous oxide (FN₂O) fluxes to their work. It is written mainly for prospective and early-career flux scientists: graduate students, postdocs, and new principal investigators planning their first non-CO₂ flux system.
It draws on materials assembled by the FLUXNET-Coop CH₄/N₂O Data Processing Committee. Jump to the guide →
What you will find here is shorter and more informal: why these gases behave differently from CO₂, what to think about first, which processing steps tend to matter most, which open tools people already use, and where the science is still being worked out.

title: Getting started with FCH₄ and FN₂O
text:
Why a separate getting-started guide?
Eddy-covariance methods for carbon dioxide and energy are comparatively mature. CH₄ and N₂O fluxes are different in ways that matter for processing. They are often smaller and noisier, and they can be episodic: N₂O can pulse after fertilizer and rain, and CH₄ can be released in short bursts. Those properties change how you:

detect the time lag between the gas analyzer and the sonic anemometer,
filter spikes and outliers without deleting real emission events,
decide whether a friction-velocity (u*) threshold developed for CO₂ should be applied,
fill gaps in the half-hourly record, and
report uncertainty.

New groups should not have to reconstruct that advice from scattered papers and meeting notes. This site collects the committee’s public-facing guidance in one place and points you to ICOS and the literature whenever you need the full specification.

title: Getting started with FCH₄ and FN₂O
text:
Mission
The committee’s mission is to provide accessible guidelines for new investigators, support the inclusive growth of the FLUXNET CH₄ and N₂O community, improve the standardization of data processing, and, over the longer term, contribute reference practices that can inform measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) uses of these fluxes.

title: Getting started with FCH₄ and FN₂O
text:
Four objectives

Better quality control. Improve quality control and quality assurance for CH₄ and N₂O fluxes, both before half-hourly fluxes are computed (high-frequency, raw-data processing) and afterward (half-hourly QC/QA).
Open resources. Share open resources for instrument setup and for reproducible processing.
Useful ancillary data. Identify the ancillary measurements that most help people interpret, gap-fill, and compare CH₄ and N₂O fluxes.
Practical guidance for new PIs. Offer best-practice guidance on site selection, systems and maintenance, ancillary measurements, high-frequency preprocessing, half-hourly post-processing, and how this work connects to global FLUXNET science.

title: Getting started with FCH₄ and FN₂O
text:
How the guide is organized


High-frequency data
From the analyzer and sonic anemometer to 30-minute fluxes: time lag, despiking, spectral corrections, and quality flags.


Half-hourly processing
QC/QA of 30-minute output, the open question of u* filtering, gap-filling, and uncertainty.


Ancillary variables
The extra measurements that make CH₄ and N₂O time series interpretable: water, redox, soils, vegetation, and management.

title: Getting started with FCH₄ and FN₂O
text:
How this relates to ICOS
If you run or plan an ICOS station, start with the ICOS instruction and discuss site-specific choices with the ICOS Ecosystem Thematic Centre. The ICOS instruction itself builds on:

Nemitz, E., Mammarella, I., Ibrom, A., et al. (2018). Standardisation of eddy-covariance flux measurements of methane and nitrous oxide. International Agrophysics 32, 517–549. doi:10.1515/intag-2017-0042
Mammarella, I., et al. (2020). Protocol for non-CO₂ eddy covariance measurements, QA/QC, data processing and gap-filling. RINGO H2020 Project Deliverable D3.5. Available from the ICOS RINGO deliverables page.

This site deliberately does not repeat ICOS rules about when CH₄ or N₂O measurements are mandatory at Class 1 stations, approved sensors, inlet geometry, calibration schedules, or file submission. It is meant to sit beside that guidance and help people getting started anywhere in the FLUXNET community.

title: Getting started with FCH₄ and FN₂O
text:
A note on open questions

Not everything is settled. Several important choices are not yet standardized for non-CO₂ fluxes. Two big ones are whether a CO₂-derived u* threshold should be applied to FCH₄ and FN₂O, and how random, u*, and gap-filling uncertainties should be combined when fluxes are aggregated to daily, seasonal, or annual totals. The guide says so plainly and points to current options rather than inventing a single “correct” recipe.

title: Getting started with FCH₄ and FN₂O
text:
Acknowledgment
This resource draws on the work of the FLUXNET-Coop CH₄/N₂O Data Processing Committee. We thank FLUXNET-Coop and everyone who has contributed time, code, data, and workshop energy to the committee. See the Network page for more about the community.

title: Network
text:
The FLUXNET-Coop CH₄/N₂O Data Processing Committee is a volunteer community of flux scientists working on how methane and nitrous oxide eddy-covariance data are collected, processed, and shared.
This page describes the community in aggregate only. Individual names appear solely when a person who is already on the private committee contact list chooses to be listed, using the form below.

title: Network
text:
Community snapshot
These approximate figures come from the committee’s 2026 summary of activities. They describe the community as a whole; they are not a membership roll.


~41 people have taken part in committee activities


~22 in North America


~15 in Europe


~2 in South America


~2 in Asia and Oceania


The community spans career stages. Roughly, it includes about 12 professors or other senior researchers, about 10 mid-career scientists, about 10 postdoctoral or other early-career researchers, about 5 PhD students or other junior researchers, and about 4 people working in industry or other roles.

title: Network
text:
What people work on
Committee work is organized around three areas, which map directly onto the sections of the guide:

High-frequency (raw-data) preprocessing: instrumentation and the path from roughly 10 Hz data to 30-minute fluxes.
Half-hourly post-processing: QC/QA, spike and outlier handling, u*, gap-filling, and uncertainty.
Ancillary variables: the extra measurements that support interpretation, gap-filling, and comparison across sites.

Shared interests that come up across these areas include processing very small or negative fluxes along the upland–wetland continuum, urban methane perspectives, and machine-learning gap-filling that can eventually align with community pipelines such as ONEFlux.

title: Guide overview
text:
This guide complements ICOS; it does not replace it. For installation geometry, approved sensors, maintenance, calibration, and ICOS file submission, use the official documents:

ICOS instructions for CH₄ and N₂O turbulent fluxes — Nicolini et al. (2024), doi:10.18160/61J9-4MMK
Nemitz et al. (2018), International Agrophysics, doi:10.1515/intag-2017-0042
Mammarella et al. (2020), RINGO Deliverable D3.5 (ICOS RINGO deliverables)
Forthcoming: paper from the 2026 Volkswagen Foundation workshop (Hannover). Citation and link will be added when available.

title: Guide overview
text:
The typical path
A typical path from a new CH₄ or N₂O analyzer to an annual budget looks like this:

Plan the site and system. Choose a site and an instrument setup appropriate to the flux size you expect, and follow your network’s hardware rules (for ICOS stations, that means the ICOS instruction).
Collect high-frequency data. Record synchronized wind and gas data, commonly at 10 Hz.
Compute fluxes. Calculate 30-minute (or 60-minute) fluxes, taking particular care with time lag, despiking, and spectral corrections.
Quality-control the half-hourly fluxes. Do not blindly reuse every default that was tuned for CO₂.
Decide on u*. Decide, transparently, what you will do about low-turbulence (low u*) periods. This is still an active discussion for CH₄ and N₂O.
Gap-fill. Fill gaps in the series. Here that means imputing missing values in one site’s time series, not spatial upscaling.
Report uncertainty and collect ancillary data. Estimate and report uncertainty, and collect the ancillary measurements you will need to interpret and gap-fill the fluxes.

title: Guide overview
section: Where each step lives in this guide
text:
Where each step lives in this guide


High-frequency data collection and processing
Steps 1–3. Instruments, time lag, wavelets, despiking, spectral corrections, and software.


Half-hourly processing
Steps 4–7. QC/QA, outliers and pulses, u*, gap-filling, and uncertainty.


Ancillary variables
Step 7 and beyond. What to measure alongside the fluxes, for CH₄ and for N₂O.

title: Guide overview
section: Why CH₄ and N₂O need extra care
text:
Why CH₄ and N₂O need extra care
Compared with CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O fluxes are often smaller relative to instrument noise and more episodic. The same building blocks apply, but the emphasis shifts:

Low signal-to-noise makes time-lag detection and the limit of detection more important.
Bursts and pulses (CH₄ ebullition, N₂O after fertilizer and rain) can be mistaken for spikes or non-stationarity and filtered out.
u* filtering and uncertainty do not yet have community-standard answers for these gases.
Drivers differ. Water, redox, substrate, vegetation, and management often matter more than light and temperature alone, which shapes both interpretation and gap-filling.

title: Guide overview
text:
How to use this guide
Read the pages in order if you are planning a new system, or jump to the page for the step you are working on. Each page ends with a short checklist or a list of open questions. Wherever this guide is brief, follow the links to ICOS and the literature for the full detail.

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
Once you have 30-minute FCH₄ or FN₂O, the post-processing chain is similar in outline to CO₂ work and different in the details. Committee discussions organized the chain this way:

Quality-control the 30-minute output.
Optionally, build the best available ancillary time series (see Ancillary variables).
Address u*, gap-filling, and uncertainty.

The output of EddyPro (or an equivalent raw-data processor) is typically the starting file. Many groups then finish the workflow in R, Python, or MATLAB.

ICOS and the RINGO D3.5 protocol (Mammarella et al., 2020; ICOS RINGO deliverables) describe QA/QC, u* filtering, and gap-filling for CH₄ and N₂O in more depth. If you contribute to ICOS, follow the ICOS instruction. This page is a getting-started summary.

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
Once you have 30-minute FCH₄ or FN₂O, the post-processing chain is similar in outline to CO₂ work and different in the details. Committee discussions organized the chain this way:

Quality-control the 30-minute output.
Optionally, build the best available ancillary time series (see Ancillary variables).
Address u*, gap-filling, and uncertainty.

The output of EddyPro (or an equivalent raw-data processor) is typically the starting file. Many groups then finish the workflow in R, Python, or MATLAB.

ICOS and the RINGO D3.5 protocol (Mammarella et al., 2020; ICOS RINGO deliverables) describe QA/QC, u* filtering, and gap-filling for CH₄ and N₂O in more depth. If you contribute to ICOS, follow the ICOS instruction. This page is a getting-started summary.

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
A practical QC/QA sequence
This sequence reflects common practice discussed by the committee. Thresholds are often site-specific. The goal is a transparent, stepwise procedure, not a single universal set of cut-offs.

Start from well-computed fluxes. Use a predetermined, narrow lag-search window and a default (nominal) lag (see the high-frequency page).
Remove only the physically impossible. Apply a coarse minimum/maximum filter only for physically impossible outliers. There is no universal “typical range” for CH₄ or N₂O; fluxes vary from near-zero uptake to large pulses, so set any bounds for your own site.
Apply standard quality flags. Use the Mauder and Foken (2004) / SSITC flags. Many groups retain quality classes 0 and 1.
Filter on diagnostics. Screen for incomplete records, low signal strength, implausible flux variances, closed-path flow rate, sonic pitch, implausible time lags, and unreasonably large spectral correction factors.
Filter on wind direction where masts, buildings, or other obstacles contaminate part of the fetch.
Propagate shared filters. Some filters apply across traces: if a period is rejected for one reason (for example a bad flow rate), remove every flux that depends on it.

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
Outliers and pulses
Because CH₄ and N₂O can be both very small and highly variable, it is easy to delete real events or to keep impossible spikes. Getting-started guidance from the committee:

Iterate, semi-automatically. Base the screening on the range you reasonably expect at your site and on the temporal character of the series: relatively steady, strongly seasonal, or pulsed.
Watch the defaults. At sites with low background fluxes plus short bursts (N₂O after fertilizer, or CH₄ ebullition), disable EddyPro’s default CO₂-oriented outlier filter. That default can remove exactly the events you care about.
Look at the data. After automatic screening, inspect the time series. A stepwise procedure plus quality flags is more defensible than a single hidden threshold.

Open tools people use for visualization and cleaning:

diive (Python)
Biomet.net and Calculation_Procedures (UBC Micromet)
A public wet-prairie processing workflow: atmos-flux-data

Useful papers:

Vitale et al. (2020), Biogeosciences, on a robust data-cleaning procedure for eddy-covariance fluxes (doi:10.5194/bg-17-1367-2020)
Langford et al. (2015), AMT (doi:10.5194/amt-8-4197-2015)
Thomas et al. (2011), Biogeosciences 8, 1595–1613, which discusses spike detection for CO₂ and energy fluxes in detail (doi:10.5194/bg-8-1595-2011)

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
Friction velocity (u*)

Open question. Whether a u* threshold developed from CO₂ (NEE) should be applied to FCH₄ and FN₂O is not settled. Applying the CO₂-derived threshold is one option used in the community, but it is not established as correct for these gases.

A useful analogy comes from FLUXNET carbon and energy processing, where sensible and latent heat fluxes are not u*-filtered in the same way as NEE (Pastorello et al., 2020, Scientific Data, doi:10.1038/s41597-020-0534-3). CH₄ and N₂O may behave more like those energy fluxes at some sites and more like CO₂ at others.
What to do for now:

If you apply a u* filter, say so, show how the threshold was chosen, and consider reporting a sensitivity test.
If you do not apply one, say that too.

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
Gap-filling
Gap-filling here means imputing missing values in a single site-level time series. It is not interpolation in the casual sense, not forecasting, and not spatial upscaling.
Getting-started points from committee discussions:

Machine-learning ensembles are the current direction for community CH₄ products. Random forests and XGBoost are often sufficient; more elaborate architectures are not automatically better.
Community direction. The committee has committed to machine-learning gap-filling for FLUXNET-CH₄ version 2.0, with longer-term interest in aligning with ONEFlux.
Realistic validation. Use cross-validation that inserts artificial gaps similar in length and timing to the gaps you actually have, not only random point-wise holdouts.
Time predictors matter. At most sites, generic temporal predictors help: day of year or season encoded as sine and cosine terms, and other smooth temporal markers.
Pick metrics carefully. Choose error metrics that respect both short-term pulses and longer-term totals. A method that matches the mean but smears out events may look good on one score and poor on another.
Calibrated uncertainty. The uncertainty of filled values can be calibrated (for example with Platt scaling). Whether that calibrated error should replace a separately estimated random uncertainty is still being discussed.

About MDS. Marginal distribution sampling (MDS), as widely used for CO₂, is not automatically the best default for CH₄ or N₂O, especially when fluxes are pulsed or gaps are long. If you use MDS, document why.
Public tools and papers:

fluxgapfill — Irvin et al. (2021), Agricultural and Forest Meteorology 308–309, 108528, doi:10.1016/j.agrformet.2021.108528
methane-gapfill-ml
Kim et al. (2020), Global Change Biology, on gap-filling approaches for eddy-covariance CH₄ fluxes, doi:10.1111/gcb.14845
Moffat et al. (2007), Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, a classic comparison of CO₂ gap-filling methods and useful background, doi:10.1016/j.agrformet.2007.08.011
Dengel et al. (2013), Biogeosciences 10, 8185–8200, which extended neural-network gap-filling to CH₄ fluxes from high-latitude wetlands, doi:10.5194/bg-10-8185-2013

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
Uncertainty
For CO₂, community tools such as REddyProc already separate several uncertainty terms and show how to aggregate them (see the REddyProc aggregated-uncertainty vignette and the MPI-BGC FAQ).
For CH₄ and N₂O, the same ingredients are discussed, but they are not yet standardized:

Random measurement uncertainty, including serial correlation (Hollinger and Richardson, 2005, Tree Physiology, doi:10.1093/treephys/25.7.873).
Uncertainty from the choice of u* threshold, if a threshold is applied.
Uncertainty from gap-filling, for example the spread across models or across gap-filling runs.
How those terms combine when you report a daily, seasonal, or annual total.
How to combine CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O when someone wants a net greenhouse-gas budget. Adding variances is only valid if the errors are independent, so do not treat that as automatic.

A transparent first step is to report each term you can estimate and to say clearly which terms you could not yet quantify. There is no single official non-CO₂ uncertainty recipe yet.

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
Remaining questions

Still being worked out:

Are CO₂-style random-uncertainty estimators the best available for CH₄ and N₂O?
Is gap-filling uncertainty partly already contained in the spread across u* scenarios, or should it be estimated separately?
How should very long gaps (for example, longer than about three months, which MDS often will not fill) be handled?
How should uncertainties be communicated when people later compute net greenhouse-gas budgets?

title: Half-hourly processing
text:
A short half-hourly checklist

Write down every filter and threshold you apply, in order.
Turn off CO₂-tuned defaults (such as EddyPro’s default outlier filter) at pulsed sites, and say so.
Inspect the screened time series by eye before gap-filling.
State whether you applied a u* filter, and how the threshold was chosen.
Validate gap-filling with realistic artificial gaps.
Report each uncertainty term you can estimate, and name the ones you could not.
